title: Number of Pairs Satisfying Inequality
description: Brute force to optimized: reducing a two-array inequality to a single derived array, then counting pairs with a Fenwick tree scan.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2 of equal length, and an integer diff, count the number of pairs (i, j) with 0 <= i < j < n such that nums1[i] minus nums1[j] is less than or equal to nums2[i] minus nums2[j] plus diff.

blocks.text: Rearranging nums1[i] - nums1[j] <= nums2[i] - nums2[j] + diff gives (nums1[i] - nums2[i]) <= (nums1[j] - nums2[j]) + diff. Defining arr[k] = nums1[k] - nums2[k], the condition becomes simply arr[i] <= arr[j] + diff, a single-array pairwise comparison.

blocks.title: Analogy: Comparing Net Scores
blocks.text: Picture each index as a player with a "net score" (nums1 minus nums2). The original two-array inequality is really just asking: is an earlier player's net score within "diff" of (or below) a later player's net score? Once you compute everyone's net score, it becomes one simple comparison per pair.

blocks.caption: Algebraic rearrangement turns the two-array inequality into a single derived array comparison

blocks.text: arr = [nums1[k]-nums2[k]] = [1, 0, 4]. Valid pairs (i,j) with arr[i] <= arr[j] + 1: (0,1): 1<=0+1 true; (0,2): 1<=4+1 true; (1,2): 0<=4+1 true. Total = 3.

Before counting pairs directly, notice the algebraic rearrangement collapses the two-array condition into a single derived array, turning this into the well-known "count pairs i<j with arr[i] <= arr[j] + diff" pattern, solvable with a Fenwick tree while scanning left to right.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the two-array form is misleading: once you move all i-indexed terms to one side and all j-indexed terms to the other, the condition becomes a single-array comparison, arr[i] <= arr[j] + diff, where arr[k] = nums1[k]-nums2[k].

Why a left-to-right scan with a Fenwick tree works: processing j in increasing order means every arr[i] for i
Handling negative values: since arr[k] can be negative, all values are shifted by a fixed constant before being used as Fenwick tree indices, so every index stays non-negative.

The core idea: algebraic rearrangement first, then a standard left-to-right Fenwick-tree counting scan.

Compute arr[k] = nums1[k]-nums2[k] for every k. Scan j from left to right, querying the Fenwick tree (shifted to handle negatives) for the count of previously-inserted values <= arr[j]+diff, then insert arr[j].

blocks.caption: Scan left to right; query the Fenwick tree for matches so far, then insert the current value

codes.python:
def number_of_pairs(nums1, nums2, diff):
    n = len(nums1)
    arr = [nums1[k] - nums2[k] for k in range(n)]
    shift = 200000  # arr[k] can range roughly -1e5..1e5
    size = 400001
    bit = [0] * (size + 2)

    def update(i):
        i += 1
        while i <= size + 1:
            bit[i] += 1
            i += i & (-i)

    def prefix(i):
        if i < 0:
            return 0
        i += 1
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += bit[i]
            i -= i & (-i)
        return s

    count = 0
    for j in range(n):
        bound = min(arr[j] + diff + shift, size)
        count += prefix(bound)              # earlier values satisfying arr[i] <= arr[j]+diff
        update(arr[j] + shift)
    return count

blocks.text: After the algebraic rearrangement, the problem becomes exactly "count pairs i<j with arr[i] <= arr[j]+diff", the standard "count of valid earlier elements" pattern. Scanning left to right guarantees that when j is processed, the Fenwick tree contains exactly the arr values for all i<j, so a single prefix-sum query up to arr[j]+diff (after shifting to handle negative values) gives the correct count in one step.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log range), one Fenwick query and update per index.
Space: O(range) for the Fenwick tree array.

blocks.text: Number of Pairs Satisfying Inequality is a strong example of "algebra first, data structure second": recognizing that a two-array inequality collapses into a single derived array is what unlocks the standard Fenwick-tree counting technique.

blocks.text: If the interviewer says "this inequality mixes two arrays at two indices", think: rearrange algebraically into a single derived array, then apply the standard pair-counting Fenwick tree technique.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the rearrange-plus-Fenwick-tree approach runs in O(n log range) time and O(range) space.

items: Pattern: algebraic rearrangement into a single derived array, then a standard Fenwick-tree pair-counting scan.
Core Idea: arr[k] = nums1[k]-nums2[k] reduces the condition to arr[i] <= arr[j]+diff; scan left to right, querying and inserting into a Fenwick tree.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n log range) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the two-array inequality is really a single-array comparison in disguise.
Interview Difficulty: the algebra is the hard part; the Fenwick-tree counting technique itself is standard once recognized.
One line memory trick: subtract the arrays first, then count pairs with a Fenwick tree.
